title: Fibroids, food and supplements
question_forms: Which foods feed or shrink fibroids?
tradition_says: Many women are told to cut red meat, dairy or sugar to stop fibroids growing, or to drink green tea or take herbs to shrink them.

layer1.plain_answer: No food has been shown to shrink fibroids. In Black women, a high glycaemic index diet was only weakly linked to fibroid risk. Five trials of vitamin D in other populations found smaller fibroids, and one tiny trial of green tea extract found the same; both need larger trials. See a doctor for heavy bleeding.

do.text: See a doctor if fibroids cause heavy or painful periods; treatment is not needed without symptoms.
Ask about a vitamin D supplement: the NHS says people with African, African-Caribbean or South Asian backgrounds should consider one through the year.
Eat a balanced diet with plenty of fruit and vegetables, as for everyone.
Know that being overweight is a risk factor the UK's NHS lists for fibroids.

avoid.text: Treating heavy bleeding with food or supplements alone: iron deficiency anaemia is a known complication.
Taking green tea extract tablets as a fibroid treatment: the only trial I found was a pilot of 39 women in Egypt.

see_someone_when: Heavy periods, pain or pressure from fibroids that affect daily life (doctor).
Tiredness, breathlessness or pale skin with heavy periods (doctor, for a blood count).
Bleeding between periods or after sex (doctor).

tested.population: 21,861 premenopausal Black women in the Black Women's Health Study, followed 1997-2007
tested.finding: During 162,604 person-years, 5,800 fibroid cases were diagnosed. Dietary glycaemic index was weakly associated with fibroid risk overall (highest against lowest quintile 1.09, 95% CI 0.99-1.19; P for trend 0.04), with stronger links in women under 35 for glycaemic load (1.18) and in college-educated women for glycaemic index (1.17).

source.authors: Radin RG, Palmer JR, Rosenberg L, Kumanyika SK et al

tested.note: Questionnaire diet; the authors call the findings something that warrants further study.

tested.population: 511 women with fibroids in 5 randomised trials of oral vitamin D (256 treated, 255 on placebo)
tested.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
tested.finding: Vitamin D supplementation significantly decreased fibroid size (standardised mean difference -0.48, 95% CI -0.66 to -0.31) and raised serum vitamin D, with a larger effect in trials lasting more than 8 weeks. The authors say larger well-designed trials are needed for other outcomes.

source.authors: Alsharif SA, Baradwan S, Alshahrani MS, Khadawardi K et al

tested.note: Trials were not in Black women; I did not read which countries or whether low-certainty.

tested.population: 39 women aged 18-50 with symptomatic fibroids (33 completed), Egypt
tested.design: Pilot double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial of green tea extract (EGCG)
tested.finding: Fibroid volume fell significantly in the green tea extract group (22 women) while it rose 24.3% in the placebo group (11 women). Symptom severity fell 32.4%, quality of life improved 18.5%, haemoglobin rose 0.7 g/dL and monthly blood loss fell from 71 to 45 mL. No adverse effects were observed.

source.authors: Roshdy E, Rajaratnam V, Maitra S, Sabry M et al

tested.note: Pilot with a 2:1 split and small groups; funding not checked.

tier_driver: That vitamin D or green tea extract shrinks fibroids: a meta-analysis of five small trials of vitamin D and one pilot of 39 women for green tea, none in Black women.
tier_note: Trials in other populations, small and not rated for certainty; the only Black-population food data are an observational cohort with a weak association; would move with a trial in Black women.
harm_note: No harm signal found in the abstracts read. The pilot reported no adverse events in 39 women and a small safety study of 39 women found no liver injury at the dose used, but both are tiny.
evidence_summary: No food is proven to shrink fibroids. In 21,861 Black women, a diet with a higher glycaemic index was weakly linked to fibroid risk. A meta-analysis of five trials in other populations found vitamin D lowered fibroid size, and a pilot of 39 women in Egypt found green tea extract reduced volume and bleeding; neither was in Black women and both call for larger trials. The UK's NHS lists being overweight as a risk factor and says fibroids need treatment only when they cause symptoms.
measured_variables: Fibroid size or volume by ultrasound; incident fibroids by ultrasound or surgery
Self-identified race in the cohort, a stand-in
gaps: Untested or not opened: whether any food or supplement changes fibroid growth in Black women in a trial (my search found none); red meat, dairy and sugar claims (no source opened); the FRIEND trial of green tea extract was seen as a protocol title only; liver safety of green tea extract in women (a 39-woman study found none, but doses are not given here); drug interaction. The NHS vitamin D line is general advice for the African and Caribbean background, not advice about fibroids.
